sect1.title: Firewall Configuration and Network Security
sect1.para: A properly configured firewall is essential for protecting your mail server from unauthorized access while allowing legitimate mail traffic. This section covers firewall configuration, port forwarding, and security hardening measures.

sect2.title: Understanding Required Ports
sect2.para: Before configuring the firewall, it's important to understand which ports your mail server needs to have open. The table below summarizes the ports used in our setup:

row.entry: External (for receiving mail from other servers)

caution.para: Do not open ports 110 (POP3) or 143 (IMAP) as these are unencrypted protocols. Only use the secure variants (995 for POP3S if needed, 993 for IMAPS).

sect2.title: Configuring SuSEfirewall2
sect2.para: OpenSuSE 11.4 and 12.1 use SuSEfirewall2 as their default firewall. This can be configured either through YaST or by editing configuration files directly.

sect3.title: Firewall Configuration via YaST
sect3.para: The easiest way to configure the firewall is through YaST:

listitem.para: Open YaST and select "Security and Users" → "Firewall"
In the "Allowed Services" section, add the following services:
If needed, add HTTP to redirect to HTTPS
For SSH access, add "Secure Shell Server" but consider restricting to specific IP addresses

sect3.title: Manual Firewall Configuration
sect3.para: For more control, edit the firewall configuration file directly at /etc/sysconfig/SuSEfirewall2:
sect3.programlisting:
# Open ports for mail server FW_SERVICES_EXT_TCP="25 80 443 587 993"
# Optionally restrict SSH to specific networks FW_SERVICES_EXT_TCP_SECURE="22" FW_TRUSTED_NETS="192.168.1.0/24"
# Enable logging of dropped packets for security monitoring FW_LOG_DROP_CRIT="yes" FW_LOG_DROP_ALL="no"
sect3.para: After editing, restart the firewall:
Verify the firewall is running:

sect2.title: Configuring firewalld (OpenSuSE 12.1+)
sect2.para: Newer OpenSuSE versions may use firewalld instead of SuSEfirewall2. If your system uses firewalld, configure it as follows:
sect2.screen: $> sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=smtp $> sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=smtp-submission $> sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=imaps $> sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https $> sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http $> sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=ssh
sect2.para: If a service isn't predefined, add ports directly:

sect2.title: Router Port Forwarding
sect2.para: If your mail server is behind a router (as is typical for home servers), you must configure port forwarding on your router to direct incoming traffic to your mail server.
The exact procedure varies by router manufacturer, but generally:

listitem.para: Log into your router's administration interface (typically via web browser)
Find the "Port Forwarding" or "Virtual Server" section
Create port forwarding rules for each required port:
Save the configuration and reboot the router if required

caution.para: Many ISPs block outgoing connections on port 25 to prevent spam. However, they typically allow incoming connections on port 25 (for receiving mail) and outgoing connections on port 587 (for sending mail). This is one reason we configure Postfix to accept submissions on port 587.

Some residential ISPs also block incoming port 25 connections. If this is the case, you won't be able to receive mail directly from other mail servers, and you'll need to use a mail relay service or upgrade to a business internet connection.

sect2.para: To test if port forwarding is working from outside your network:
sect2.screen: $> telnet your-external-ip 25 $> telnet your-external-ip 587 $> telnet your-external-ip 993
sect2.para: If the connection succeeds, port forwarding is working. If it times out or is refused, check your router configuration and firewall rules.

sect2.title: Installing and Configuring Fail2ban
sect2.para: Fail2ban is a security tool that monitors log files for suspicious activity (such as repeated failed login attempts) and automatically blocks offending IP addresses. This is essential protection against brute-force attacks on your mail server.

sect3.title: Installing Fail2ban
sect3.para: Enable and start Fail2ban:
sect3.screen: $> sudo systemctl enable fail2ban $> sudo systemctl start fail2ban

sect3.title: Configuring Fail2ban for Mail Services
sect3.para: Create a local configuration file at /etc/fail2ban/jail.local:
sect3.programlisting:
[DEFAULT] # Ban for 1 hour bantime = 3600 # Look for failures in 10 minute window findtime = 600 # Ban after 5 failures maxretry = 5
# Protect Dovecot IMAP/POP3 [dovecot] enabled = true port = imap,imaps,pop3,pop3s logpath = /var/log/mail.warn
# Protect Postfix SMTP [postfix] enabled = true port = smtp,submission logpath = /var/log/mail.warn
# Protect SASL authentication [postfix-sasl] enabled = true port = smtp,submission logpath = /var/log/mail.warn
# Protect Apache/Roundcube [apache-auth] enabled = true port = http,https logpath = /var/log/apache2/error_log
# Protect SSH (recommended) [sshd] enabled = true port = ssh logpath = /var/log/messages
sect3.para: Restart Fail2ban to apply the configuration:
Check Fail2ban status:
To see banned IPs for a specific jail:
sect3.screen: $> sudo fail2ban-client status dovecot $> sudo fail2ban-client status postfix
sect3.para: To manually unban an IP address if you accidentally locked yourself out:

sect3.title: Testing Fail2ban
sect3.para: To verify Fail2ban is working, you can deliberately trigger a ban from another machine:

listitem.para: Try to connect to your IMAP server with wrong credentials 6 times
Check if the IP was banned:
Try to connect again - the connection should be refused

listitem.screen: $> sudo fail2ban-client set dovecot unbanip YOUR-TEST-IP

sect2.title: Additional Security Hardening
sect2.para: Beyond firewall configuration, several additional measures can improve your mail server's security posture.

sect3.title: File Permissions
sect3.para: Ensure sensitive configuration files have appropriate permissions:
sect3.screen: $> sudo chmod 600 /etc/postfix/main.cf $> sudo chmod 600 /etc/dovecot/conf.d/*.conf $> sudo chmod 600 /etc/fetchmailrc $> sudo chmod 600 /etc/ssl/private/*.key
sect3.para: Private key files should never be world-readable:
sect3.screen: $> sudo ls -l /etc/ssl/private/ # Should show permissions like: -rw------- (600)

sect3.title: Disable Unnecessary Services
sect3.para: Review what services are running and disable those not needed:
For a minimal mail server, you typically only need:
Disable unnecessary services:
sect3.screen: $> sudo systemctl disable <service-name> $> sudo systemctl stop <service-name>

sect3.title: Rate Limiting in Postfix
sect3.para: Configure Postfix to rate-limit connections to prevent abuse. Add to /etc/postfix/main.cf:
sect3.programlisting:
# Limit connection rate to 100/hour from same IP smtpd_client_connection_rate_limit = 100
# Limit number of simultaneous connections per client smtpd_client_connection_count_limit = 10
# Limit recipient addresses per message smtpd_recipient_limit = 50
# Limit error rate before disconnect smtpd_soft_error_limit = 2 smtpd_hard_error_limit = 5
sect3.para: Reload Postfix after changes:

sect3.title: Monitoring Failed Login Attempts
sect3.para: Regularly review logs for suspicious activity:
sect3.screen:
# Check for failed Dovecot logins $> sudo grep "auth failed" /var/log/mail.warn | tail -20
# Check for Postfix authentication failures $> sudo grep "authentication failed" /var/log/mail.warn | tail -20
# See unique IPs with failed attempts $> sudo grep "auth failed" /var/log/mail.warn | \ awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
sect3.para: High numbers of failed attempts from the same IP indicate a brute-force attack. Fail2ban should be catching these, but manual review helps identify patterns.

sect3.title: Using DNSBL (DNS Blocklists)
sect3.para: Configure Postfix to reject mail from known spam sources using DNS blocklists. Add to /etc/postfix/main.cf:
sect3.programlisting: smtpd_recipient_restrictions = permit_mynetworks permit_sasl_authenticated reject_unauth_destination reject_rbl_client zen.spamhaus.org reject_rbl_client bl.spamcop.net reject_rbl_client b.barracudacentral.org
sect3.para: This will check connecting mail servers against these blocklists and reject mail from listed IPs.

caution.para: Be cautious with DNSBL usage - overly aggressive blocking can reject legitimate mail. Monitor your logs after implementing DNSBL to ensure you're not blocking wanted email.

sect2.title: Testing Network Security
sect2.para: After configuring your firewall and security measures, it's important to verify everything is working correctly.

sect3.title: Port Scanning from External Network
sect3.para: From a computer outside your network (or using an online port scanner), verify only the expected ports are open:
You should see only: 25, 80 (if enabled), 443, 587, and 993 as open. All other ports should show as filtered or closed.

sect3.title: Verifying Firewall Rules
sect3.para: Check which ports are actually listening:
Verify iptables rules (SuSEfirewall2 uses iptables internally):
Look for rules accepting traffic on your mail ports.

sect3.title: Testing Mail Flow Through Firewall
sect3.para: Test that you can send and receive mail through the firewall:

listitem.para: From an external location, send a test email to your server
Configure a mail client on an external network to connect via IMAPS/SMTPS
Verify you can both send and receive mail
Access Roundcube via HTTPS from an external network
